title: Scaling Failure and Capacity Controls
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to diagnose how overload can become a cascading failure and select capacity controls that protect useful work. After completing it, learners can distinguish admission control, bounded queues, load shedding, graceful degradation, and retry control, then combine them into a defensible overload response.
objectives: Explain how overload, rising latency, retries, and resource exhaustion can reinforce one another.
Identify whether admission control, a bounded queue, load shedding, graceful degradation, or retry control addresses a given overload symptom.
Design a provider-neutral overload response that preserves capacity for selected useful work.
Evaluate capacity controls by observing latency, errors, queue growth, rejected work, and completed useful work.

sections.title: Level and foundations
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes basic familiarity with requests, latency, error rates, and queues, but it does not assume experience with a particular provider or operational tool.

Capacity is the amount of work a service can complete while meeting its intended performance and reliability goals. Demand becomes overload when incoming work exceeds the service's available capacity. Scaling failure occurs when the system cannot add or preserve effective capacity quickly enough to handle that demand.

sections.title: From overload to cascading failure
paragraphs: Overload can form a reinforcing cycle. As available resources become saturated, requests take longer to complete. More work remains in progress or waits in queues, consuming additional resources. Clients may retry failed or slow requests, adding demand while the service is least able to absorb it.

A cascading failure occurs when overload in one component contributes to overload or failure elsewhere. Merely accepting every request does not guarantee useful progress. Protecting the system requires limiting admitted work and preserving enough capacity to complete selected requests.

sections.title: Capacity controls
paragraphs: Admission control decides whether new work may enter based on available capacity or an explicit limit. Rejecting excess work early can be safer than accepting work that will wait until it times out or consumes resources without completing.

A bounded queue limits how much work may wait. Once the queue reaches its bound, additional work is rejected or shed according to a defined policy. A bound prevents waiting work from growing without limit and makes overload behavior more predictable.

Load shedding deliberately rejects some work when capacity is exhausted. A useful shedding policy preserves higher-priority or more critical work rather than treating all requests as equally important.
Graceful degradation reduces the cost or scope of work while retaining a useful result. This differs from scaling because it lowers demand on constrained resources instead of adding capacity.

Retry control limits the extra demand caused by repeated attempts. Retries should not be treated as free because every attempt consumes capacity. When failures are caused by overload, unrestricted retries can intensify the condition.

sections.title: Selecting and combining controls
paragraphs: Choose a control by matching it to the failure mechanism. Use admission control when too much work enters the system, a bounded queue when waiting work accumulates, load shedding when only part of the demand can be served, graceful degradation when cheaper work can still provide value, and retry control when repeated attempts amplify demand.

These controls are complementary. A service can restrict admission, keep its queue bounded, preserve critical requests through load shedding, offer a reduced response through graceful degradation, and limit retries at the same time.

A sound policy defines which work is preserved and which work may be rejected before an incident occurs. Without that decision, an overloaded service may spend scarce capacity on low-value work while critical work fails.

sections.title: Evaluating the response
paragraphs: Evaluate controls under representative overload conditions rather than considering request acceptance alone. Observe latency, error rates, queue growth, rejected work, and completed useful work. Rejection can be an intended protective outcome when it prevents a larger failure and allows selected requests to finish.

A successful response keeps resource use and queues within deliberate limits, avoids retry amplification, and preserves the categories of work the policy identifies as most important. If latency and queue depth continue to rise while useful completions fall, the controls are not containing overload.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes the reinforcing overload cycle presented in this module?
choices: Longer request times increase waiting or in-progress work, and retries add more demand.
Early rejection always increases queue size, which creates more capacity.
Graceful degradation adds resources until every request receives the full result.
A bounded queue accepts unlimited waiting work while reducing latency.
questions.explanation: The module explains that saturation can increase request duration and accumulated work, while retries add demand during the overload.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a bounded queue during overload?
choices: To guarantee that every request is eventually accepted
To prevent waiting work from growing without limit
To make every request equally critical
To replace all admission and retry controls
questions.explanation: A bounded queue caps waiting work and rejects or sheds additional work after reaching that bound.

questions.prompt: A service is overloaded, and repeated attempts are adding substantial demand. Which control directly addresses that amplification?
questions.explanation: Retry control directly limits the additional demand created by repeated attempts.

questions.prompt: When can rejecting work be an intended protective outcome?
choices: When rejection prevents a larger failure and preserves capacity for selected useful work
Only when no request categories have different priorities
Whenever the queue has no defined bound
questions.explanation: The module states that deliberate rejection can protect the service and allow selected requests to complete.
